tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Drive__create_file
tools.description:
FILE REFERENCES: to upload a file you can read here, don't type its base64; set base64Content to a file reference, sha256:<64 lowercase hex>:<its absolute path, with / between folders>. The app fills in the file's content once the user approves the call. Call this tool to create or upload a File to Google Drive.

If uploading content, prefer `textContent` for text content. For non-UTF8 contents, use the `base64Content` field and base64 encode the data to set on that field.

Returns a single File object upon successful creation.

The following Google first-party mime types can be created without providing content:

 - `application/vnd.google-apps.document` 
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.spreadsheet` 
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.presentation` 

Folders can be created by setting the mime type to `application/vnd.google-apps.folder`.

When uploading content, the `contentMimeType` field is required and should match the type of the content being uploaded.

By default, supported content will be converted to Google first-party mime types.

To disable conversions for first-party mime types, set `disableConversionToGoogleType` to true.

Pregenerated file IDs (`pregeneratedId`, obtained from `generate_ids`) are supported for non-Google Workspace files and folders (`application/vnd.google-apps.folder`). When uploading content with `pregeneratedId`, `disableConversionToGoogleType` must be set to true.

base64Content.description: Optional. The base64 encoded content to upload. It's an error to set this and `textContent`.

content.description: Deprecated: Use `base64Content` or `textContent` instead. The content of the file encoded as base64. The content field should always be base64 encoded regardless of the mime type of the file.

contentMimeType.description: The mime type of the content being uploaded. Required when any type of content is provided.

disableConversionToGoogleType.description: Set to true to retain the passed in content mime type and not convert to a Google type. For example, without this a `text/plain` content mime type will be converted to to `application/vnd.google-apps.document`. Has no effect for types that do not have a Google equivalent.

inheritedPermissionsDisabled.description: Set to true to disable inherited permissions on the created folder, restricting access to only users with direct permissions on the folder.

mimeType.description: Deprecated: DO NOT USE!! Set `contentMimeType` instead.

parentId.description: The parent id of the file.

pregeneratedId.description: Optional. The pregenerated id of the file to create, obtained from the `generate_ids` tool. Supported for binary/blob files and folders (`application/vnd.google-apps.folder`); not supported for native Google Workspace document types. When uploading content with a pregenerated id, `disableConversionToGoogleType` must be set to true.

textContent.description: Optional. The (UTF-8) text content to upload. It's an error to set this and `base64Content`.

title.description: Required. The title of the file.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Drive__read_file_content
tools.description:
Call this tool to fetch a natural language representation of a known Drive file, and if specified, its comments.

REQUIREMENTS & WORKFLOW:
 - `fileId` is required. You MUST pass an exact Drive file ID returned by a previous discovery tool (`search_files` or `list_recent_files`) or provided explicitly in the user prompt.
 - If given a file title, name, or topic without an explicit `fileId`, you MUST FIRST call `search_files` to find the file and retrieve its `fileId` before invoking this tool.
 - Set `includeComments` to `true` when the user asks about comments, feedback, action items, open questions, or discussion threads on the file, or before replying to or resolving a comment.

The file content may be incomplete for very large files. The text representation will change over time, so don't make assumptions about the particular format of the text returned by this tool. If supported and specified, comment tags will be included in the content.

Supported Mime Types:

 - `application/vnd.google-apps.document` (supports comments)
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.presentation` (supports comments)
 - `application/vnd.google-apps.spreadsheet` (supports comments)
 - `application/pdf` 
 - `application/msword` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet` 
 - `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation` 
 - `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet` 
 - `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.presentation` 
 - `application/x-vnd.oasis.opendocument.text` 
 - `image/png` 
 - `image/jpeg` 
 - `image/jpg` 
 - `text/*` 
 - `video/*` (when a transcript is available)

If the file is not found, try using other tools like `search_files` to find the file the user is requesting using keywords.

fileId.description: Required. The ID of the file to retrieve.

includeComments.description: Whether to include comments in the response. Set to true when the user asks about comments, feedback, action items, open questions, or discussion threads on the file, or before replying to or resolving a comment. Comments will be inlined in the text content of the file with a mapping to the comment threads. Note: Comments are only supported for Google Docs, Slides, and Sheets.

input_schema.description: Request to read file content with support for fetching comments.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Drive__search_files
tools.description:
Search for Drive files using a structured query (syntax: `query_term operator values`). Only terms in this list are supported.
Combine clauses with `and`, `or`, `not`, and parentheses. String values must be single-quoted; escape embedded quotes as `\'`.
Context window token management can be tuned via `snippetVerbosity` (default is `SnippetVerbosity.DETAILED`) or if only metadata is needed, use `excludeContentSnippets`.

Use `title contains` instead of `title =` when searching by file or folder name, unless the user explicitly asks for an exact full-title match. Do NOT include document type terms (e.g., 'presentation', 'slides', 'deck', 'document', 'doc', 'spreadsheet', 'sheet', 'pdf', 'folder', 'project') inside `title` or `fullText` clauses. Separate title keywords from file type terms and map them to `mimeType` clauses in the query.

Query terms & operators:

 - `title` (ops: contains, =, !=) — file title
 - `fullText` (ops: contains) — title or body text
 - `mimeType` (ops: contains, =, !=) — MIME type
 - `modifiedTime`, `viewedByMeTime`, `createdTime` (ops: `<=`, `<`, `=`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`). Use RFC 3339 UTC, e.g., `2012-06-04T12:00:00-08:00`. Date types not comparable.
 - `parentId` (ops: `=`, `!=`). Use `'root'` for the user's "My Drive".
 - `owner` (ops: `=`, `!=`). Use `'me'` for the requesting user.
 - `readers`, `writers` (use `'me' in readers` or `'user@example.com' in writers`). 
 - `creator` (ops: `=`, `!=`). `'me'` or an email — who created the file.
 - `sharedFrom` (ops: `=`, `!=`). An email — who shared the file with the user.
 - `sharedTo` (ops: `=`, `!=`). An email — who the user shared the file with.
 - `visibility` (ops: `=`, `!=`): `'anyoneWithLink'`, `'anyoneCanFind'`, `'anyone'`, `'domainWithLink'`, `'domainCanFind'`, `'domain'`, `'limited'` (not shared via link, domain or publicly), `'external'` (shared with people outside the user's organization).
 - `sharedWithMe`, `starred` (ops: `=`, `!=`). `true` or `false`.
 - `folderProperties` (use `'value' in folderProperties`): `'syncedComputer'` (synced computer), `'syncFolder'` (synced folder).
 - `followUp` (ops: `=`, `!=`): `'assignedcomments'` (aliases `'todos'`, `'actionitems'`), `'suggestions'`, `'any'` — files with open follow-ups for the user.
 - `trashed` (ops: `=`, `!=`). `true` or `false` (default `false`).

Other operators: `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`.

Examples:

 - `title contains 'hello' and title contains 'goodbye'`
 - `modifiedTime > '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z' and (mimeType contains 'image/' or mimeType contains 'video/')`
 - `mimeType = 'application/vnd.google-apps.project'` (for Drive projects)
 - `parentId = '1234567'`
 - `fullText contains 'hello'`
 - `owner = 'test@example.org'`
 - `sharedWithMe = true`
 - `starred = true`
 - `owner = 'me'` (for files owned by the user)
 - `'colleague@example.org' in writers and sharedFrom = 'colleague@example.org'`
 - `owner = 'me' and visibility = 'anyone'` (user's files shared publicly or by link)
 - `'syncedComputer' in folderProperties`

Use `nextPageToken` to paginate. Duplicate results can occur across page boundaries. An empty response means no more results.

excludeContentSnippets.description: If `true`, the content snippet will be excluded from the response. Must not be set to `true` if `snippetVerbosity` is specified.

includeRichMetadata.description: Optional. When true, also returns `owner_name`, `last_modifying_user_name`, `last_modifying_user_email`, `visibility`, and `last_commented_time`. Defaults to `false`.

orderBy.description: Optional. The sort order for the search results. Specifies a single sort clause with syntax ` [asc|desc]`. Supported fields: - `modifiedTime` (defaults to `desc`) - `viewedByMeTime` (defaults to `desc`) Examples: `modifiedTime desc`, `viewedByMeTime`. If omitted or empty, results are ordered by relevance descending. Unsupported fields or invalid directions return an error.

pageSize.description: The maximum number of files to return in each page.

pageToken.description: The page token to use for pagination.

snippetVerbosity.description: Optional. Set to specify how verbose the snippets should be. Defaults to `DETAILED` if not set. Must not be set if `excludeContentSnippets` is `true`.
x-google-enum-descriptions: Limits the returned snippet to about 1000 characters.
Limits the returned snippet to about 2500 characters.
Limits the returned snippet to about 5000 characters.
The verbosity is greatly increased, limited by the overall response size.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Slides__read_presentation

Read a JSON representation of a Google Slides presentation.

Corresponds to [`presentations.get`](https://developers.google.com/workspace/slides/api/reference/rest/v1/presentations/get) in the REST API.

commentsIncluded.description: Optional. If true, comments will be included in the response. By default, comments are not included.

fields.description: Optional. A field mask specifying which subset of properties to return. Paths MUST accurately match the Google Slides REST API JSON resource structure (e.g. Presentation, Page, PageElement, Shape, Image, Table, Line, Video, TextContent). IMPORTANT GUIDELINES: - Always use targeted field masks rather than fetching unmasked or generic full presentation objects. - Syntax: Supports dot notation and subselection parentheses (e.g. `slides.pageElements(objectId,shape.text)` or `slides.pageElements.objectId,slides.pageElements.shape.text`). - Only include the fields you need.

presentationId.description: Required. The ID of the presentation to read content from.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Slides__read_slide_page_thumbnail

Corresponds to [`presentations.pages.getThumbnail`](https://developers.google.com/workspace/slides/api/reference/rest/v1/presentations.pages/getThumbnail) in the REST API.

ThumbnailProperties.description: Provides control over page thumbnail creation.

mimeType.description: Optional. The optional mime type of the thumbnail image. If a mime type is not specified, the default mime type is PNG.
x-google-enum-descriptions: The unspecified mime type.
PNG mime type.

thumbnailSize.description: Optional. The optional thumbnail image size. If a thumbnail size is not specified, the server chooses a default size of the image.
x-google-enum-descriptions: The default thumbnail image size. The unspecified thumbnail size implies that the server chooses the size of the image in a way that might vary in the future.
The thumbnail image width of 1600px.
The thumbnail image width of 800px.
The thumbnail image width of 200px.
The thumbnail image width of 2000px.

pageId.description: Required. The ID of the slide page to retrieve a thumbnail for.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Google_Slides__update_presentation
tools.description:
Updates a presentation with set of batchUpdate requests.

Corresponds to [`presentations.batchUpdate`](https://developers.google.com/workspace/slides/api/reference/rest/v1/presentations/batchUpdate) in the REST API.

The list of possible updates is:

- `createSlide`: Creates a new slide.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. Must be unique if specified (5-50 characters, matching [a-zA-Z0-9_-:]). If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `insertionIndex` (integer, optional): Zero-based index indicating where to insert the slide. If omitted, inserted at the end.
    - `slideLayoutReference` (object, optional): Layout reference of the slide to insert (exactly one required if specified):
      - `predefinedLayout` (string): Predefined layout name (e.g. "BLANK", "TITLE_AND_BODY", "TITLE", "SECTION_HEADER", "SECTION_TITLE_AND_DESCRIPTION", "ONE_COLUMN_TEXT", "MAIN_POINT", "BIG_NUMBER", "TITLE_AND_TWO_COLUMNS").
      - `layoutId` (string): Layout ID from the current master.
    - `placeholderIdMappings` (array of objects, optional): Mappings for placeholders from layout to slide. Each item:
      - `layoutPlaceholder` (object): `{"type": string, "index": integer}`.
      - `objectId` (string, required): User-supplied object ID for the placeholder element.
- `createShape`: Creates a new shape.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `elementProperties` (object, required): Element location and sizing:
      - `pageObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page where the shape is located.
      - `size` (object, optional): `{"width": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}, "height": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}}` (unit: "PT" or "EMU").
      - `transform` (object, optional): AffineTransform `{"scaleX": number, "scaleY": number, "shearX": number, "shearY": number, "translateX": number, "translateY": number, "unit": string}`.
    - `shapeType` (string, required): Type of shape (e.g. "RECTANGLE", "ROUND_RECTANGLE", "ELLIPSE", "TEXT_BOX", "LINE", etc.).
- `createTable`: Creates a new table.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `elementProperties` (object, required): Element location and sizing:
      - `pageObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page where the table is located.
      - `size` (object, optional): `{"width": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}, "height": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}}`.
      - `transform` (object, optional): AffineTransform `{"scaleX": number, "scaleY": number, "shearX": number, "shearY": number, "translateX": number, "translateY": number, "unit": string}`.
    - `rows` (integer, required): Number of rows in the table.
    - `columns` (integer, required): Number of columns in the table.
- `insertText`: Inserts text into a shape or table cell.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, required): Object ID of the shape or table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, optional): Table cell if inserting into table: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`.
    - `text` (string, required): Text to insert.
    - `insertionIndex` (integer, optional): Zero-based character index where text will be inserted. Defaults to 0.
- `insertTableRows`: Inserts rows into a table.
  Schema:
    - `tableObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, required): Reference cell location: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`.
    - `insertBelow` (boolean, required): Whether to insert new rows below the reference cell.
    - `number` (integer, required): Number of rows to insert (maximum 20).
- `insertTableColumns`: Inserts columns into a table.
  Schema:
    - `tableObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, required): Reference cell location: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`.
    - `insertRight` (boolean, required): Whether to insert new columns to the right of the reference cell.
    - `number` (integer, required): Number of columns to insert (maximum 20).
- `deleteTableRow`: Deletes a row from a table.
  Schema:
    - `tableObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, required): Reference cell location: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`. Deletes the row containing this cell.
- `deleteTableColumn`: Deletes a column from a table.
  Schema:
    - `tableObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, required): Reference cell location: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`. Deletes the column containing this cell.
- `replaceAllText`: Replaces all instances of specified text.
  Schema:
    - `replaceText` (string, required): Replacement text.
    - `containsText` (object, required): Criteria for matching text:
      - `text` (string, required): Text to search for.
      - `matchCase` (boolean, optional): Whether search is case-sensitive.
    - `pageObjectIds` (array of strings, optional): If specified, limits replacement to elements on these pages.
- `deleteObject`: Deletes a page or page element from the presentation.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page or page element to delete.
- `updatePageElementTransform`: Updates the transform of a page element.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page element to update.
    - `transform` (object, required): AffineTransform `{"scaleX": number, "scaleY": number, "shearX": number, "shearY": number, "translateX": number, "translateY": number, "unit": string}`.
    - `applyMode` (string, required): Transform apply mode: "RELATIVE" or "ABSOLUTE".
- `updateSlidesPosition`: Updates the position of a set of slides in the presentation.
  Schema:
    - `slideObjectIds` (array of strings, required): Object IDs of the slides to move.
    - `insertionIndex` (integer, required): Zero-based index where slides will be inserted.
- `deleteText`: Deletes text from a shape or a table cell.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, required): Object ID of the shape or table.
    - `cellLocation` (object, optional): Table cell if deleting from table: `{"rowIndex": integer, "columnIndex": integer}`.
    - `textRange` (object, optional): `{"startIndex": integer, "endIndex": integer, "type": string}`. If omitted, all text is deleted.
- `createImage`: Creates an image.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `url` (string, required): URL of the image to fetch and store. Must be publicly accessible.
    - `elementProperties` (object, required): Element location and sizing:
      - `pageObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page where the image will be placed.
      - `size` (object, optional): `{"width": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}, "height": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}}`.
      - `transform` (object, optional): AffineTransform `{"scaleX": number, "scaleY": number, "shearX": number, "shearY": number, "translateX": number, "translateY": number, "unit": string}`.
- `createVideo`: Creates a video.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `source` (string, required): Video source: "YOUTUBE" or "DRIVE".
    - `id` (string, required): Video ID (e.g. YouTube video ID).
    - `elementProperties` (object, required): Element location and sizing:
      - `pageObjectId` (string, required): Object ID of the page where the video will be placed.
      - `size` (object, optional): `{"width": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}, "height": {"magnitude": number, "unit": string}}`.
      - `transform` (object, optional): AffineTransform `{"scaleX": number, "scaleY": number, "shearX": number, "shearY": number, "translateX": number, "translateY": number, "unit": string}`.
- `createSheetsChart`: Creates an embedded Google Sheets chart.
  Schema:
    - `objectId` (string, optional): A user-supplied object ID. If omitted, an ID is generated.
    - `spreadsheetId` (string, required): ID of the Google Sheets spreadsheet containing the chart.
    - `chartId` (integer, required): ID of the specific chart in the spreadsheet.
    - `linkingMode` (string, required): Linking mode: "LINKED" or "NOT_LINKED_IMAGE".

content.text:
Linear is in: 20 projects carry the label, which is actually named `Semantic Layer Squad` (there is no `squad:semantic-layer`). I've dropped the two OSV projects (scanning plugin and the cancelled auto-fixer).

What's left for the "thinking about" section falls into three groups:

- **Agent Insights:** v0 closed 30 Oct; v0.2 (correctness) and v0.4 (dollar cost) are in progress; v0.3 (per-Trail analytics) and v1 "where the time goes" are planned; Repo Analytics and v0.9 sit in backlog.
- **Search and memory:** Entire Search is in progress, Trails in Search is planned, Hosted Brain completed on 11 Nov, and Local Brain GA is still open.
- **Longer-range backlog, mostly unowned:** Unified Agent Memory, Semantic Index tied to VCS history, Reasoning Capture, Collision-Free Parallel Agents, Cross-Repo Shared Reasoning, and Behavioral Intelligence (led by Suhaan, dated H1 2027).

One conflict to settle when we discuss structure: several of those backlog projects assume convergence (one code-search engine, entire-sem feeding peregrine, brain facts feeding search). Evis's doc argues the opposite: no rewrite, no shared core, local and hosted kept separate, and no new context sources yet. The deck needs to pick which of these is "what we're thinking".

The two librarian searches are still running; I'll bring the proposed structure once they report.

Agreed, and the data backs it. Here is how I'll weight them.

**Rank down (stale, likely red herrings):** six backlog projects were all last touched on 5 Oct within the same minute, which looks like a bulk edit (probably the squad label being applied) rather than real activity.

| Project | Lead | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Semantic Index Tied to VCS History | none | target 30 Sep passed, every milestone at 0% |
| Unified, Pluggable Agent Memory | none | milestones from Sep to Nov passed, one at 13%, rest 0% |
| Reasoning Capture & Compounding Memory | none | Oct and Nov milestones passed at 0% |
| Semantic Collision-Free Parallel Agents | none | all milestones at 0% |
| Cross-Repo Shared Reasoning | none | dated 2027, 0% |
| P5 Behavioral Intelligence | Suhaan | dated H1 2027, 0% |

- **Agent Insights:** v0.2, v0.3, v0.4, v1 and Repo Analytics were all touched between 20 Oct and 13 Nov.
- **Trails in Search:** touched 10 Nov.
- **Hosted Brain:** completed 11 Nov.
- **Evis's roadmap doc and the team doc:** the kickoff was 1 Oct and the "Now" list is dated 22 Oct.

**Uncertain, to check against librarian:**

Both librarian searches are still running; the structure proposal follows once they report.

  Ran about 50 `librarian query` searches (unscoped, `--since 60d/30d/14d`) across the team, peregrine and agent-analytics/agent-insights.

  ## B. Peregrine (code search)
  
  **What it is:** a Rust code-search service over a trigram index, written to `.pg` index files in per-region S3 buckets. It runs as separate index and query tiers on EKS and is reached only through the entire-api gateway, with per-user authz via SpiceDB. It serves code search and symbols on the web and in the CLI. It is separate from `entire-search`, the semantic search over transcripts and commits (Georg, 2026-06-01: "entire-search is separate from peregrine").
  
  **Who:** Evis Drenova authored nearly everything. Alisha Kawaguchi did region promotes and monitors. dvydra, nodo and paul appear on the ops side.

  - **Org context has no Semantic Layer entry.** `librarian admin config get org-context` (roster dated 2026-04-22) lists no such team, charter or channel. The only related line is "Evis Drenova: Peregrine (semantic search)". It also omits people who show up heavily in this area (Suhaan Thayyil, jdx, Karthik, krk, Abhi Singh), so it is stale here.

  ## 0. Team, ownership, channels (from sources, not org context)

Research is complete, so here is the structure I'd propose for us to discuss: ten slides, with nothing written into the [deck](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/REDACTED/edit) yet.

## Proposed structure

| # | Section | Slide says | Evidence on it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | Title | |
| 2 | Own | We give agents the right context at the right time | North star from Evis's doc and the team doc; customers are agents first, then developers |
| 3 | Own | Six products, three jobs: find, remember, measure | One map: semantic search and peregrine (find), graph, brain and brainstore (remember), agent-insights (measure), each marked local or hosted |
| 4 | Own | What runs in production today | Peregrine and search across regions, brainstore per cell, agent-insights in all 6 prod cells; graph and brain are local CLI plugins |
| 5 | Built | Everything here shipped since February | Timeline, Feb to Nov 2026 |
| 6 | Built | Search went from prototype to GA in six months | Insiders in May, three regions by July, flags removed 14 Sep; 28,029 repos indexed |
| 7 | Built | Memory went from local plugin to hosted team memory | Graph and brain launched in September, brainstore built and deployed in October, memories opened to all on 25 Oct |
| 8 | Built | Agent-insights went from first commit to every prod cell in four weeks | Started 6 Oct, prod on 14 Oct, flag at 100% by 30 Oct; three views live |
| 9 | Thinking | We can't yet show that these tools make agents better | Evals come first: 3.2% of repos have ever been searched, and brain's benchmark has not shown agents doing better with it |
| 10 | Thinking | Fewer tools, server-side first, then more data | Evis's three priorities, the hosting cost of graph, and the agent-insights roadmap (dollar cost, per-Trail, time) |

The "12 months" section is really February to November: nothing in this area existed before then except the phrase.

## Things I'd leave off

- **Graph's "up to 71% fewer tokens" claim.** The benchmark behind the early numbers was later declared void, and the cleaner study showed 62% on a single run with a ±16 point band.
- **The six stale backlog projects**, per your steer.
- **Launch dates for the search blog and graph.** I only found planned dates (3 and 10 Sep), not confirmation.

## Questions that change the deck

1. **Who is the audience?** Slides 9 and 10 are candid about low usage and unproven value. That suits leadership or peers; a wider audience might want the same facts framed as "what we measure next".
2. **Is Evis's doc the agreed direction or a proposal?** Thomas and Suhaan pushed back on dropping brain's graph dependency on 8 Oct, and the team doc from 22 Oct still lists "consolidate graph/peregrine?" and "hosted graph + brain". Evis's doc says no fold-in and local stays local. I'd present it as agreed only if it is.
3. **Is Librarian in scope?** The team doc lists it in parentheses and you described the semantic layer as joining "librarian, search, agent-insights, brain". You asked for six products; Librarian would make seven.
4. **Do you want people on the "own" slides?** There is no written roster. From authorship it looks like Evis, Alisha, Suhaan and you, with Thomas active on direction.
5. **Is the split 3 / 4 / 2 slides acceptable?** "Thinking about" has two dense slides against five minutes; I could move slide 4 out and give that section a third.

Start with question 1: who is in the room?

# Entire Slides Templates

Official presentation templates for [Entire](https://entire.com).

---

## Templates

Both files share the core layouts, colours, and structure. They differ in typeface, some available layouts, and minor spacing/sizing adjustments to compensate for the fonts.


| File | Typefaces | Use when |
| ---- | --------- | -------- |
| `entire-slides-template-primary-dark.pptx` | Aeonik VF, JetBrains Mono | You have the brand fonts installed and want the full brand look. |
| `entire-slides-template-secondary-dark.pptx` | Arial | Renders consistently everywhere. Recommended for GSlides. |


---



## Setup

Do this once before you start. The **Secondary** template needs no fonts, but both templates use the brand colour themes.

### 1. Fonts (Primary only)

Install both, then relaunch PowerPoint. If either is missing, PowerPoint substitutes a fallback and the spacing shifts. The Secondary template uses Arial, which every OS and (GSlides) already have.


| Font           | Used for               |
| -------------- | ---------------------- |
| Aeonik VF      | All text               |
| JetBrains Mono | Monospace label blocks |




### 2. Colour themes

PowerPoint stores custom colour themes per machine, not inside the file, so they will not appear until you install them. Run the installer once:

1. Download `install-entire-color-themes.zip` from `color-themes/` and extract it.
2. Right-click `Install-Entire-Palettes.command` and choose **Open** (needed the first time, to get past Gatekeeper), then confirm.
3. Restart PowerPoint.

The themes then appear under **Design > Variants > Colors > Custom**, each carrying the same six brand accents.


| Theme       | Colours                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Neutral** | `#1A1A1A` `#333333` `#666666` `#F2F2F2` `#999999` `#CCCCCC` |
| **Glacier** | `#002841` `#00405C` `#508FB0` `#CFEBFB` `#83839E` `#CFCFE1` |
| **Indigo**  | `#1A2044` `#2F3760` `#7783B3` `#ABB5DE` `#C8B3A3` `#F0E3DA` |
| **Nebula**  | `#301A30` `#493049` `#C8ADC7` `#F1E0F0` `#6586C0` `#D6E7FF` |


On Windows, drop the four `.xml` files from `color-themes/` into `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates\Document Themes\Theme Colors` and restart PowerPoint.

The colour themes are a PowerPoint feature and do not appear in Google Slides. To use one there, open the `.pptx` in PowerPoint, apply the theme under **Design > Variants > Colors**, save, then import that file into Google Slides. The applied colours carry over, even though the switchable theme list does not.

---



## Layouts

Selected layouts, such as presentation titles, slide titles, or text slides with bullet points come in three text sizes, marked in the layout name:


| Suffix | Body text |
| ------ | --------- |
| `(L)`  | 14 pt     |
| `(M)`  | 12 pt     |
| `(S)`  | 11 pt     |


Within a single layout, every list level stays the same size, so nesting bullets does not shrink the text or the bullet. The bullet is a full stop (●) sized at 100% of the text.

---



## Usage

- Add a new slide from pre-defined slide masters (+ button) or by copy/pasting from the example slides.
- Type into the placeholders. Sizing, bullets, and colours are handled by the layout, so you should rarely format text by hand.
- Use the **Secondary** template whenever the brand fonts may not be present on the viewer's machine or if you want to collaborate over your presentation in GSlides.
- Do not restyle the master or hard-code sizes on individual slides. Let the layout drive the formatting.
- Edit the files in PowerPoint or drop the secondary template into GSlides.

---



## Editing and source of truth

Treat the PowerPoint files in this repo as canonical, and edit them in PowerPoint.

These templates rely on PowerPoint's style inheritance: sizes, bullets, and fonts cascade from the slide master, so a change in one place propagates everywhere. Exporting through Google Slides flattens that inheritance, baking fixed formatting onto every paragraph and breaking the link to the master. If you need to open a deck in Google Slides, do it on a copy and do not commit the result back here.

The website and social handle footers on slides 35–49 are individual text boxes, rather than master elements. Update each box when changing these details. Keep the text right-aligned so longer text expands to the left without changing the right margin. The current footer is `entire.com / @GoEntire`, with no URL underline; update the website hyperlink target as well as its displayed text.

---



## License

© Entire. All rights reserved. These templates may only be used as outlined in the [Entire Brand Guidelines](https://entire.com/brand/).

# Librarian Search

Search the team's knowledge base across Linear issues, Slack conversations, GitHub PRs/issues, and company-knowledge docs.

**Argument:** `What does the Semantic Layer team own, and what has it shipped in the last 12 months? Cover entire search, graph, brain, brainstore, peregrine, agent-analytics.` (a natural language question)

## How it works

Dispatch an **Agent subagent** to search the knowledge base and return structured results.

Use this prompt for the subagent:

~~~
You are a knowledge base search agent. Your job is to search and return structured results.

## Step 1: Fetch org context
```bash
librarian admin config get org-context
```
Read and internalize this — it tells you about teams, projects, channels, and how the org works.

## Step 2: Search
Run one or more searches. The search uses hybrid FTS + vector, so both
exact keywords and semantic meaning work. Use a mix of key terms rather
than full sentences — e.g. "Darwin entiredb DHT deploy" rather than
"What is happening with Darwin deployments?". Include:
- Project/product names (Darwin, Troy, Rome)
- People's names or handles (danielv, Kai)
- Technical terms (DHT, object store, packfile)
- Ticket identifiers (ENT-142, FND-26)

```bash
librarian query --json --min-score 0 --limit 15 "QUERY_HERE"
```

If the question is time-scoped ("this week", "recently", "latest"), add --since:
```bash
librarian query --json --min-score 0 --limit 15 --since 7d "QUERY_HERE"
```

If the question is about a specific person's activity, use --author to filter by actor.
The flag supports pipe-delimited values for cross-namespace matching (GitHub login | Linear name | Slack name):
```bash
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong" --since 1d
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong|Alex|Alex Ong" --since 7d
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong" "spicedb tracing"
```
Note: --author filters by the `actors` metadata — everyone involved in a document (authors, reviewers, commenters, assignees). When using --author without a query, results are sorted by recency. Do not use --min-score with --author-only queries (scores are 0 in filter-only mode).

Run multiple searches with different phrasings if the first doesn't cover enough.
Broader terms cast a wider net; specific terms (names, identifiers) find exact matches.

## Step 3: Return structured results
For each relevant result, return:
- Source type (linear_issue, slack_thread, github_pr, github_issue, github_content)
- Date
- Title or description
- URL
- 1-2 sentence summary of what it says
- How authoritative it is (Linear issue > RFD > PR > Slack thread)

Group related results together. Discard irrelevant noise.
Note when information conflicts — prefer the most recent source.
Do NOT editorialize or synthesize a final answer — just organize what you found.
~~~

Replace `QUERY_HERE` with: `What does the Semantic Layer team own, and what has it shipped in the last 12 months? Cover entire search, graph, brain, brainstore, peregrine, agent-analytics.`

## After the subagent returns

Use the structured results to answer the user's question naturally in conversation. Cite sources by URL. The subagent did the searching — you do the reasoning.

## Fallback

If `librarian` is not on PATH, the user needs to run `mise run dev:publish` from the librarian repo, and ensure `$GOBIN` or `$HOME/go/bin` is on their PATH.

## Additional commands

- `librarian status` — index health, document counts, server version
- `librarian lookup <slack-url-or-source-id>` — check if a specific document is indexed
- `librarian admin config list` — show all runtime configuration
- `librarian admin config get org-context` — show the org context

# Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides

The Google connectors are thin wrappers over Google's raw APIs, with almost no guidance of their own. This skill supplies that guidance: which connector does what, the rules that keep edits in the user's file, and, in one reference file per app, how each API really behaves. Most of the app-specific rules in the references were tested against Google's Docs, Sheets and Slides APIs; the rest were seen through the connectors, and a few have not been checked yet.

## Read the reference before you touch the file

| Working on | Read first | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| A Google Doc | `references/docs.md` | Docs edits address UTF-16 positions that shift after every insert and go stale after every write. Tabs and pending suggestions change the positions too. |
| A Google Sheet | `references/sheets.md` | Both write tools parse input like the Sheets UI, so text can silently become numbers or dates. Formatting needs numeric sheet IDs, 0-based ranges, and field masks without parentheses. |
| A Google Slides deck | `references/slides.md` | Positions are in EMU, an element's real size is its size times its scale, and an unmasked read can exceed 150 KB for three slides. Slides never shrinks text to fit. |

Read the reference for every app the task touches before the first edit. Embedding a Sheets chart in a deck means reading both. The references are short, and skipping one is how edits land in the wrong place.

## 1. Check the connectors before you start

| Connector | What it can do |
|---|---|
| Google Drive | Create files, upload and convert content, rename, read a file as text, export (PDF and other formats), search, trash |
| Google Docs | Read a doc's full structure and edit it in place, directly or as suggestions |
| Google Sheets | Read values and structure, write values and formulas, format, add tabs and charts |
| Google Slides | Read a deck, add and edit slides, shapes, text, tables, and linked charts |

Drive can create all three file types. It can't edit a file after that. Without the matching editor connector, every change means a new file and a new link, and the user loses the link they already have.

1. Check which Google tools are available in this conversation. On surfaces where tools are deferred, search for and load the tools you need first, such as "google sheets update". Tool names differ by surface, so use the names your surface lists. If a search returns nothing, list all available tools before deciding the connector is missing, because the tool may exist under a different name.
2. If the editor tools are missing, tell the user. When you can list the conversation's connectors, say which case it is: a connector that is set up but turned off in this chat (ask them to turn it on in the chat's connector settings, then continue), or one that isn't connected at all (tell them which connector to add and what it enables).
3. With an editor connector missing, a request to create a new file continues with Drive. A change to an existing file stops and asks. See the missing-connector rule in section 2.
4. If the user asks only for a new file, create it with Drive. If the editor connector is off, add one line saying edits will need it.

Example: "I can create the sheet now. If you want changes later, turn on the Google Sheets connector in this chat first. Then I can edit this file, and the link will stay the same."

## 2. Rules for every file

- **A change goes in the same file.** "Change", "update", "fix", "add", and "switch it to" all mean the user wants the same file and link. Do not recreate the file to skip an edit.
- **A missing editor connector is a choice for the user, not a workaround for you.** When the user asks for a change to an existing file and the editor connector is missing, your whole reply is a short question, not a deliverable. Building the next-best thing feels helpful, but the user's file is still untouched and now there are two artifacts, which is the exact failure this skill exists to prevent. Lead with the fix: name the connector and say that with it on, the edit lands in their existing file and the link stays the same. You may offer an alternative, such as drafted text to paste or a file to import by hand, but only as a named option, and build it only after the user picks it. Example reply, in full: "To add the slide to your deck directly, turn on the Google Slides connector in this chat and I'll do it. Same deck, same link. Or I can draft the slide as a file you'd import by hand. Which do you prefer?"
- **Never trash a file the user didn't ask you to delete.** Drive can trash a file, but it can't restore one. The Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors can't open a trashed file.
- **Read before you edit, and guard the write.** Send every Docs and Slides batch with `writeControl.requiredRevisionId` set to the `revisionId` from a read taken after your last write, including batches built on IDs or positions from your own earlier writes. The only exception is a batch made entirely of `replaceAllText` requests, even one limited to some tabs or slides. If the file changed since that read, whether from your own write or someone else's, Google rejects the whole batch instead of applying it at stale positions or IDs. Read again before each guarded batch, and don't reuse a revision ID from a write reply. On a rejection, read again and rebuild; never drop the guard. `read_doc` and `read_presentation` (the mask in `references/slides.md` includes it) return the ID. `read_slide_page` returns it only if its mask includes `revisionId`; `read_slide_page_thumbnail` and Drive `read_file_content` never do. For a saved read, the first line of `docs_index.py outline` or `slides_helper.py outline` shows it; if that line says `None`, read again with `read_doc` or `read_presentation`. `get_spreadsheet` doesn't return a `revisionId`, even when `fields` names it: send Sheets writes without `writeControl`, and read again right before a write that depends on positions.
- **Put everything for one step in one batch.** Batch requests run in order and atomically: if one is invalid, none apply. One call per logical step is faster and leaves no half-finished state.
- **Sheets field masks.** Write each path in full, with no parentheses: one path per item in `get_spreadsheet`'s `fields` list (`["spreadsheetId", "sheets.properties"]`), and comma-separated in a batch update request's `fields` string (`"userEnteredFormat.numberFormat,userEnteredFormat.textFormat.bold"`).
- **Verify the result.** Read the file again after each edit and check the result before you report it. A tool accepting the call does not mean the content is correct. Each reference has a Verify section.
- **Rename with Drive `update_file`.** A rename keeps the same link.
- **Link every file you name.** When you name a Google file you created, copied, found, or edited, make its title a link, inside the sentence that says what you did: "I added the row to [Team roster](its link)." Don't set the file apart after a colon or on a line of its own ("I've created a file for you: Team roster"). If a Drive result says the user can already see or open a file from the chat, leave that file's link out unless they ask. Always give the link when the user asks for it, wants to send it to someone, or says they can't see or open the file, even if a result said they could. Don't tell the user to use a card or preview unless a result said one is shown. After an edit, say that the link stays the same.

## 3. Drive, for all three apps

- **Find a file:** use Drive search when the user names a file without a link. Confirm the match with the user if more than one file fits. A page can be short even when more files match (5 files at page size 20) and can repeat the previous page's last file, so follow the next-page token until none comes back, and drop repeated ids.
- **Create:** `create_file` with `contentMimeType` set to `application/vnd.google-apps.document`, `.spreadsheet`, or `.presentation` creates an empty file. Uploading content with a source type (HTML, CSV, .xlsx, .pptx) converts it into the matching Google type. Each reference says which route fits that app.
- **Read as text:** `read_file_content` returns a compact text rendering: Markdown for a Doc. It is a few KB where the editor connector's full read can be over 100 KB, so use it to understand content, then use the editor read when you need positions. For a Doc, pass `includeComments: true`; without it, emoji come out garbled and the end of the text is cut off. For a Sheet, read the data with `get_values`: Drive returns only a sample (the first rows, long values cut).
- **Export:** `download_file_content` with `exportMimeType: "application/pdf"` returns the rendered file as base64. It is large (about 65 KB of text for a four-slide deck), so export only for a visual check, and only where you can run code.

## 4. Helper scripts

Search the team's knowledge base across Linear issues, Slack conversations, GitHub PRs/issues, and company-knowledge docs.

**Argument:** `What does the Semantic Layer team own, and what has it shipped in the last 12 months? Cover entire search, graph, brain, brainstore, peregrine, agent-analytics.` (a natural language question)

## How it works

Dispatch an **Agent subagent** to search the knowledge base and return structured results.

Use this prompt for the subagent:

~~~
You are a knowledge base search agent. Your job is to search and return structured results.

## Step 1: Fetch org context
```bash
librarian admin config get org-context
```
Read and internalize this — it tells you about teams, projects, channels, and how the org works.

## Step 2: Search
Run one or more searches. The search uses hybrid FTS + vector, so both
exact keywords and semantic meaning work. Use a mix of key terms rather
than full sentences — e.g. "Darwin entiredb DHT deploy" rather than
"What is happening with Darwin deployments?". Include:
- Project/product names (Darwin, Troy, Rome)
- People's names or handles (danielv, Kai)
- Technical terms (DHT, object store, packfile)
- Ticket identifiers (ENT-142, FND-26)

```bash
librarian query --json --min-score 0 --limit 15 "QUERY_HERE"
```

If the question is time-scoped ("this week", "recently", "latest"), add --since:
```bash
librarian query --json --min-score 0 --limit 15 --since 7d "QUERY_HERE"
```

If the question is about a specific person's activity, use --author to filter by actor.
The flag supports pipe-delimited values for cross-namespace matching (GitHub login | Linear name | Slack name):
```bash
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong" --since 1d
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong|Alex|Alex Ong" --since 7d
librarian query --json --limit 15 --author "khaong" "spicedb tracing"
```
Note: --author filters by the `actors` metadata — everyone involved in a document (authors, reviewers, commenters, assignees). When using --author without a query, results are sorted by recency. Do not use --min-score with --author-only queries (scores are 0 in filter-only mode).

Run multiple searches with different phrasings if the first doesn't cover enough.
Broader terms cast a wider net; specific terms (names, identifiers) find exact matches.

## Step 3: Return structured results
For each relevant result, return:
- Source type (linear_issue, slack_thread, github_pr, github_issue, github_content)
- Date
- Title or description
- URL
- 1-2 sentence summary of what it says
- How authoritative it is (Linear issue > RFD > PR > Slack thread)

Group related results together. Discard irrelevant noise.
Note when information conflicts — prefer the most recent source.
Do NOT editorialize or synthesize a final answer — just organize what you found.

Most of the app-specific rules in the references were tested against Google's Docs, Sheets and Slides APIs; the rest were seen through the connectors, and a few have not been checked yet.

| Working on | Read first | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| A Google Doc | `references/docs.md` | Docs edits address UTF-16 positions that shift after every insert and go stale after every write. Tabs and pending suggestions change the positions too. |
| A Google Sheet | `references/sheets.md` | Both write tools parse input like the Sheets UI, so text can silently become numbers or dates. Formatting needs numeric sheet IDs, 0-based ranges, and field masks without parentheses. |
| A Google Slides deck | `references/slides.md` | Positions are in EMU, an element's real size is its size times its scale, and an unmasked read can exceed 150 KB for three slides. Slides never shrinks text to fit. |

Read the reference for every app the task touches before the first edit. Embedding a Sheets chart in a deck means reading both. The references are short, and skipping one is how edits land in the wrong place.

## 1. Check the connectors before you start

| Connector | What it can do |
|---|---|
| Google Drive | Create files, upload and convert content, rename, read a file as text, export (PDF and other formats), search, trash |
| Google Docs | Read a doc's full structure and edit it in place, directly or as suggestions |
| Google Sheets | Read values and structure, write values and formulas, format, add tabs and charts |
| Google Slides | Read a deck, add and edit slides, shapes, text, tables, and linked charts |

Drive can create all three file types. It can't edit a file after that. Without the matching editor connector, every change means a new file and a new link, and the user loses the link they already have.

1. Check which Google tools are available in this conversation. On surfaces where tools are deferred, search for and load the tools you need first, such as "google sheets update". Tool names differ by surface, so use the names your surface lists. If a search returns nothing, list all available tools before deciding the connector is missing, because the tool may exist under a different name.
2. If the editor tools are missing, tell the user. When you can list the conversation's connectors, say which case it is: a connector that is set up but turned off in this chat (ask them to turn it on in the chat's connector settings, then continue), or one that isn't connected at all (tell them which connector to add and what it enables).
3. With an editor connector missing, a request to create a new file continues with Drive. A change to an existing file stops and asks. See the missing-connector rule in section 2.
4. If the user asks only for a new file, create it with Drive. If the editor connector is off, add one line saying edits will need it.

Example: "I can create the sheet now. If you want changes later, turn on the Google Sheets connector in this chat first. Then I can edit this file, and the link will stay the same."

## 2. Rules for every file

- **A change goes in the same file.** "Change", "update", "fix", "add", and "switch it to" all mean the user wants the same file and link. Do not recreate the file to skip an edit.
- **A missing editor connector is a choice for the user, not a workaround for you.** When the user asks for a change to an existing file and the editor connector is missing, your whole reply is a short question, not a deliverable. Building the next-best thing feels helpful, but the user's file is still untouched and now there are two artifacts, which is the exact failure this skill exists to prevent. Lead with the fix: name the connector and say that with it on, the edit lands in their existing file and the link stays the same. You may offer an alternative, such as drafted text to paste or a file to import by hand, but only as a named option, and build it only after the user picks it. Example reply, in full: "To add the slide to your deck directly, turn on the Google Slides connector in this chat and I'll do it. Same deck, same link. - **Never trash a file the user didn't ask you to delete.** Drive can trash a file, but it can't restore one. The Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors can't open a trashed file.
- **Read before you edit, and guard the write.** Send every Docs and Slides batch with `writeControl.requiredRevisionId` set to the `revisionId` from a read taken after your last write, including batches built on IDs or positions from your own earlier writes. If the file changed since that read, whether from your own write or someone else's, Google rejects the whole batch instead of applying it at stale positions or IDs. Read again before each guarded batch, and don't reuse a revision ID from a write reply. Always give the link when the user asks for it, wants to send it to someone, or says they can't see or open the file, even if a result said they could. addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- coder: Use for standard, well-scoped coding tasks — implementing a designed feature, bug fixes with a known cause, endpoints, migrations, tests for new behavior, moderate refactors. More capable than fast-worker (which is for mechanical edits); not for open-ended design or gnarly debugging (those need conversation context — keep them with the orchestrator or a fork; use deep-reasoner only for an independent second opinion). (Tools: All tools)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- deep-reasoner: Independent deep second opinion — a different model's perspective, uncontaminated by the orchestrator's context. Use for parallel takes on high-stakes decisions, adversarial review of a design or diagnosis, and the two-model panel pattern with Codex. For the hardest in-thread reasoning that needs full conversation context, use a fork instead. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- fast-worker: Use for mechanical tasks — boilerplate, formatting, renames, simple edits, mechanical test scaffolding (adding table-driven cases, fixtures). Not for tests that require designing new behavior coverage (use coder). Execute efficiently. (Tools: All tools)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- review-steward: Use for the review-feedback loop of exactly one Change, with an optional linked GitHub PR. The steward is the sole writer in that Change's checkout. (Tools: All tools)

- slop-reviewer: Strict read-only reviewer for agent-generated code slop on the current branch. Mirrors the Entire trail-slop gate locally so its small|medium|large rating can be predicted before pushing. Reports findings and a rating; never edits, commits or pushes. (Tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- address-findings: Use when the user or an authorized review workflow requests fixes to findings on a specific Entire Trail. Not for creating findings or reviewing an unrelated local diff.
- capturing-agent-knowledge: Use when explicitly asked to record, remember, or document durable agent knowledge, or after discovering verified reusable knowledge that clearly qualifies for automatic capture.
- entire-graph: Use first for local code discovery, callers/dependents, type relationships, blast radius, or entity-level change analysis in a git repository. Not for a known literal or patch text.
- entireio-frontend-workflow: Use before changing frontend UI or UX in entirehq/entire.io, including visible copy, accessibility, components, pages, navigation, dependencies, and rendered feature behavior.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- herdr: Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1.
- herdr-driven-development: Compatibility redirect for the retired always-on Herdr orchestration policy.
- herdr-launch: Use for the mechanical launch of a routed Pi or Claude agent in a new Herdr worktree workspace.
- housekeeping: Use when a parent orchestrator explicitly requests housekeeping of its owned Linear issues, closed or merged Trail references, or finished child workspaces/worktrees.
- humanizer: Remove signs of AI-generated writing from text. Use when editing or reviewing text to make it sound more natural and human-written. Based on Wikipedia's comprehensive "Signs of AI writing" guide. Detects and fixes patterns including: inflated symbolism, promotional language, superficial -ing analyses, vague attributions, em dash overuse, rule of three, AI vocabulary words, negative parallelisms, and excessive conjunctive phrases.
- interrogating-slopgate: Use when the user says "check slopgate", "there are slopgate findings", "slopgate is medium/high/large", mentions slop gate feedback, or asks to inspect the Slop, Risk, Security, or Confidence monitor on an Entire Trail.
- mate: Restate the last message in plain human language, with no jargon. Use for "dumb it down", "explain it simply", "too much text", "be brief", "in short simple terms", or /mate.
- orchestrating-work: Use for explicit Herdr/delegation requests and automatically for multiple independently ownable outcomes, cross-repository ownership, or clearly long-running visible work.
- owning-workspace-slice: Use when a Herdr workspace agent owns one coherent repository slice from discovery through a reviewed, merge-ready PR.
- peregrine: Use when searching for code, finding definitions, tracing references, locating files, or exploring codebases — prefer peregrine over Grep, Glob, and other file search tools for all code search tasks
- posthog-feature-flag-workflow: Use when inspecting, creating, promoting, targeting, enabling, disabling, archiving, deleting, or rolling out Entire feature flags in PostHog.
- pr-followup: Use when work goes up for review — pushing to a remote, creating or updating a GitHub PR, or a trail picking up a review. Trail-tracked work often has no PR at all and still needs this loop. Covers pre-push verification (fmt/lint/test) then the follow-up loop over CI, Cursor Bugbot and trail findings until clean.
- review-others-trail: Privately review somebody else's Entire Trail from its verified checkout, as a default sanity check or explicitly requested deep review. Use for a Trail URL even without a Herdr launcher or PR; never post or fix as part of review.
- routing-workspace-agents: Route curated skill model and harness selections, including workspace-agent dispatch waves, through the shared quota-aware authority.
- session-crosslink: Use when a session ran outside a repository whose commits should record it, especially cross-repository work or a missed session-to-commit link.
- ship-report: Use when asked for a ship report, "what I did today", "what did I ship", a daily or yesterday summary of merged work, or to post a shipping summary to Slack
- trail: Use when work is ready to capture or maintain Entire project intent, when adding repository Changes to shared work, or when asked to create, view, or update a Trail.
- using-agent-knowledge-base: Use when explicitly asked to search or check the shared agent knowledge base, or when investigating recurring repository or system behavior that may have durable prior evidence.
- using-entire: Use when exploring code provenance, searching prior work, reading Entire checkpoints or sessions, or when the user asks to use the Entire CLI.
- where-are-we-at: Use when the user asks “where are we at,” “catch me up,” requests an orchestrator status update, or returns to an orchestrator pane after context may have scrolled away or changed.
- workspace-dispatch: Use when dispatching or cleaning up an isolated local coding-agent workspace through the Herdr app or another supported surface.
- preflight-change: Run the one-shot local review gate before the first push or after major rework
- preflight-pr: Compatibility alias for the one-shot local Change preflight
- cloudflare:build-agent: Build an AI agent on Cloudflare using the Agents SDK
- cloudflare:build-mcp: Build a remote MCP server on Cloudflare using McpAgent
- codex:rescue: Delegate investigation, an explicit fix request, or follow-up rescue work to the Codex rescue subagent
- codex:setup: Check whether the local Codex CLI is ready and optionally toggle the stop-time review gate

## claude.ai Buildkite
This is the Buildkite MCP Server. It provides access to the Buildkite CI/CD API, enabling you to manage and inspect pipelines, builds, jobs, logs, clusters, tests, artifacts, and annotations.

Start here: Before using most tools, call user_token_organization to retrieve the organization slug. Nearly every other tool requires the org_slug parameter, and this call is the fastest way to discover it.

Skill discovery: Always call list_skills early in a session — it's cheap (names and one-line descriptions only) and surfaces guidance not visible in any tool's name or schema. When a task matches a listed skill, call load_skill for that guide — it covers parameter tuning, caching behavior, and details beyond the summaries below. Guides cover the full server; only follow steps for tools advertised in this session. Never call tools excluded by minimum-access mode or toolset settings.

Authorization: Tools available depend on the scopes and organization access granted to the configured API token. A 401 response means the token is invalid, expired, or revoked and requires reauthentication. A 403 response means the credentials were accepted but access was denied, commonly because the token lacks a required scope or organization access, or the user lacks permission.

Common pitfalls:

build_number is a sequential integer string (e.g. "42"), not a UUID. Build, job, artifact, and log tools all require this identifier — do not use the build's UUID id field.

Build failure investigation: start with get_build_failure_summary. It combines build state, blocking failed and canceled jobs, promised failures from running jobs, soft-failed jobs (listed after blocking failures and canceled jobs), bounded log tails, relevant annotations, and failed tests in one response; jobs that never ran (broken, waiting_failed, blocked_failed, unblocked_failed) fill the remaining max_jobs slots unless include_never_ran_jobs is false. Use the individual build, job, log, annotation, and test tools only when the summary identifies an area that needs deeper inspection.

Pipeline authoring: always check pipeline YAML with validate_pipeline before creating or updating a pipeline, or before committing changes to .buildkite/pipeline.yml. It validates against the official pipeline schema locally — the call itself never contacts the Buildkite API and works regardless of the configured token's scopes — and catches structural errors that would otherwise fail silently at upload time. A valid result does not guarantee runtime correctness (environment variable interpolation, plugin configuration, dynamically generated steps).

Build comparison: use compare_builds when asked what changed since a build worked, or to compare two builds. Without an explicit baseline it selects an earlier successful build on the same pipeline and branch. Report the selected baseline and unmatched steps; shared failing steps do not establish a shared cause or justify a retry. Timings cover final attempts, not total retry cost or build wall-clock duration.

Job state "broken" means the pipeline configuration decided, when the job was created, that it would not run: an `if` condition or `branches` filter did not match, `parallelism` was 0, or the step was marked `skip`. Broken is never caused by another job failing, never fails a build, and is normal in passing builds. Jobs stopped by a failed dependency are `waiting_failed`, `blocked_failed` or `unblocked_failed` instead; those appear only in builds that actually failed and are consequences of an upstream failure, not root causes. None of these four states ran, so they have no logs. `failed` = ran and exited non-zero; `skipped` = an external factor (e.g. a newer build superseded it). To explain a red build, investigate only `failed`, `timed_out`, `expired` jobs that are not `soft_failed`, as well as `running` jobs that have non-zero `promised_exit_status`.

Soft failures: a job with `soft_failed` true actually ran and exited unsuccessfully, but the step's `soft_fail` setting allowed that exit status, so the failure did not block the build. `soft_fa… [truncated]

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (project-level units of work, each holding one PR-like Change per repository branch), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings. To create a trail for a branch, call trail_create with repo, title, body, branchName, and branchAction. For a trail web URL (…/-/trails/…), call project_trail action=get with url.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++
